title: Bastardica
text: Bastardica type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-29 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high daring-fireball labor-displacement Summary Bastardica is a browser tool that remixes existing fonts into new ones by substituting every Nth glyph from a different source font, delivered as a normal OpenType file. The swap rides on a liga contextual substitution registered for every script, so browsers and design tools enable it by default; everything runs locally via Pyodide and fontTools, and it can pull all Google Fonts into its dropdowns or use free sources like Velvetyne and Font Squirrel. Practical tips: use Y-offset and scale to align mixed glyphs, and pick prime-number strides so three or more mixed fonts collide rarely every 5th and every 7th glyph intersect on the 35th, and the first font wins . Caveat: mixing two fonts creates a derivative work, so source licenses matter for commercial use; Bastardica itself adds no conditions. Highlights - Browser tool that remixes fonts by substituting every Nth glyph from another font - Output is a normal OpenType file using a liga contextual substitution enabled by default - Runs fully locally with Pyodide and fontTools; can load all Google Fonts - Use Y-offset and scale effects to align mixed glyphs - Prime-number strides minimize collisions when mixing 3+ fonts 5th and 7th collide on the 35th - Mixing fonts creates a derivative work - check source licenses for commercial use - Inspired by Times New Bastard and Easy Pete Source Read the original story https://bastardica.mitpit.com/ Related pages AI, jobs and displacement ../concepts/labor-displacement.md

title: Mistral and partners release Apollo, an LLM for Ancient Greek
text: Mistral and partners release Apollo, an LLM for Ancient Greek type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high techmeme mistral external-evaluation Summary The Austrian Academy of Science, in partnership with French AI lab Mistral and technology services firm Sail Reply, is releasing Apollo, billed as the world's first advanced large language model for Ancient Greek. Trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words drawn from manuscripts, papyri and inscriptions, the model will be freely available to academics through a chatbot interface. Apollo is built to fill the gaps in damaged papyrus fragments with the most statistically likely words or passages, work that until now required a rare specialist to identify word divisions, date the document and weigh socio-political context. The model adapts to the dialect in front of it, supplementing Homeric Greek for Homer and Doric for inscriptions. Scholars expect it to speed up reconstruction so they can focus on what documents mean, though they caution it will mostly surface mundane letters and contracts rather than lost plays by Sophocles. Highlights - Austrian Academy of Science, Mistral and Sail Reply built Apollo, an LLM for Ancient Greek. - Trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words from manuscripts, papyri and inscriptions. - Free to academics through a chatbot interface. - Fills gaps in damaged papyri with the most statistically likely words or passages. - Adapts by dialect: Homeric Greek for Homer, Doric for inscriptions, says papyrologist Anna Dolganov. - Sail Reply partner Dimitris Vlitas: unlocking knowledge this way 'was unthinkable a year ago.' - Oxford's Armand D'Angour: a machine suggesting three candidate words per gap 'would speed up matters considerably.' - UCL's Stephen Colvin cautions most unrestored papyri are mundane, so no new Sophocles plays should be expected. Source Read the original story https://www.wired.com/story/apollo-ai-model-ancient-greek-secrets-papyrus/ Related pages Mistral ../entities/mistral.md · External AI evaluation ../concepts/external-evaluation.md

title: SAIR's Open Math Model initiative
text: SAIR's Open Math Model initiative type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai Summary Terence Tao announced that SAIR, the Foundation for Science and AI Research he co-founded last year with private donors to support responsible AI use in mathematics and the sciences independent of major AI companies, is launching an Open Math Model initiative. SAIR has been negotiating with academic and industry partners to build open-weight models for science plus open-source tooling for using both open and closed LLMs in scientific applications. The rollout was meant to be gradual, a few pilot projects over coming months, but given current events and high demand for open models, the announcement is being accelerated to today even though key planning is still underway. SAIR started small, podcasts, short events and competitions, recently received support from XTX Markets for its next competition round, and is now expanding in scale, ambition and logistical capacity. title: New bill to protect American citizens access to AI – Please read and share
text: New bill to protect American citizens access to AI – Please read and share type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary A pair of discussion-draft bills - one federal, one for Minnesota - published at righttorun.us propose a statutory right to 'acquire, possess, develop, share, access and operate computational resources and AI systems for lawful purposes,' while categorically stripping government of the power to restrict an AI system because of how capable it is. The drafts argue that capability-based rules - compute thresholds, parameter counts, benchmarks, autonomy proxies - reliably sort people: agencies and large institutions absorb compliance costs while individuals, small businesses and researchers get degraded access. The framing is deliberately absolute. An earlier draft allowed capability restrictions under a compelling-interest and narrow-tailoring test; the current versions drop it, on the logic that conceding the balancing test concedes the right. Misuse stays fully punishable - fraud, intrusion, weapons development, harm to children remain illegal with or without AI - and export controls like the 2025 AI Diffusion Framework are expressly left alone. Other burdens on the right get an RFRA-modeled strict-scrutiny test with added requirements. The proposal, which asks readers to share it, cites EO 14110's revoked 10^26-operations reporting threshold and California and New York's frontier-model duties as the trend it answers. Highlights - Two discussion drafts federal + Minnesota at righttorun.us: a statutory right to run computation and AI for lawful purposes. - Core move: government loses all power to restrict a system for its capability - compute thresholds, parameter counts, benchmarks, autonomy proxies all void. - Categorical by design: an earlier draft allowed compelling-interest exceptions; the current one withholds the authority entirely. - Misuse remains punishable: fraud, intrusion, weapons development, harm to children stay illegal with or without AI. - Export controls such as the 2025 AI Diffusion Framework are expressly out of scope. - Other burdens face an RFRA-modeled compelling-interest / least-restrictive-means test. - Targets capability-based regimes: EO 14110's revoked 10^26 threshold, California and New York frontier-model duties. - Argues capability rules sort people: big

title: Show HN: AI·rete·RAG – a Rete rule engine decides, RAG explains why
text: Show HN: AI·rete·RAG – a Rete rule engine decides, RAG explains why type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news anthropic agentic-systems external-evaluation ai-safety-incidents ai-policy-regulation Summary In a Show HN post, the maker of ai-rete-rag describes running a Rete rule engine and RAG in series: a pure-Python Rete engine evaluates YAML rules against the facts and issues the verdict same facts, same verdict, every time, with salience-based conflict resolution , while RAG retrieves passages from the user's own policy documents and an LLM only writes the plain-English explanation, citing those passages. title: Distributing LLM inference in DwarfStar
text: Distributing LLM inference in DwarfStar type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high antirez apple nvidia xiaomi deepseek small-specialist-models compute-buildout Summary antirez surveys the economics of local LLM inference and what they mean for his DwarfStar engine. High-end NVIDIA setups are out of reach for most, and the RAM shortage makes a hypothetical M5 Ultra Mac Studio unlikely. A Mac Studio M3 Ultra 512GB runs DeepSeek v4 PRO - even at 2-bit quantization - at 150 t/s prefill and about 10-13 t/s decoding for roughly 12k total, while today's best deal is arguably a laptop: an M5 Max 128GB MacBook runs DeepSeek v4 Flash and Mimo V2.5 at about 500 t/s prefill and 35-40 t/s decoding for 6-7k. That hardware reality makes distributed inference interesting: what can two or four Macs do together? He walks through the classic options - splitting layers across machines simple activations-only traffic, and micro-batching can even speed up prefill , splitting MoE experts across machines over Apple RDMA activations are tiny; suits models with large routed experts , and tensor parallelism, which he rules out without NVLink-class interconnects. His preferred third way is newer: run two different open-weight models shared-nothing on separate machines and ensemble them, picking the lower-perplexity continuation or combining logits - an implicit two-expert mixture that recent papers suggest genuinely beats either model alone. Highlights - Mac Studio M3 Ultra 512GB: DeepSeek v4 PRO at ~150 t/s prefill, 10-13 t/s decode, ~12k total - Even 2-bit quantized, DeepSeek v4 PRO 'resists very well' - it wrote a C compiler - RAM shortage makes an M5 Ultra unlikely; an M5 Max 128GB laptop is the current best deal - M5 Max: DeepSeek v4 Flash / Mimo V2.5 at ~500 t/s prefill, 35-40 t/s decode, for 6-7k - Distribution option 1: split layers across machines; activations-only traffic, micro-batched prefill - Option 2: split MoE experts over Apple RDMA; tiny activations, suits big routed experts - Tensor parallelism ruled out - interconnects are far too slow - Option 3: two different models on two machines, ensembled by perplexity or logits Source Read the original story http://antirez.com/news/167 Related pages Apple ../entities/apple.md · NVIDIA ../entities/nvidia.md · Xiaomi ../entities/xiaomi.md · DeepSeek ../entities/deepseek.md · Small and sp

title: Pirate Face Rescues LLM Models from Deletion
text: Pirate Face Rescues LLM Models from Deletion type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Pirate Face is a decentralized mirror for open AI models: it turns Hugging Face models, datasets and other open artifacts into checksum-verified torrents with magnet links, so no single host can take them down. Every torrent carries a web-seed BEP-19 pointing at the original Hugging Face file, so downloads work even with zero peers, and every weight file keeps its official Hugging Face SHA-256 so any copy can be verified byte-for-byte against tampering. The pitch is permanence plus drop-in compatibility: pipelines can point at Pirate Face with the same paths and API, just a different endpoint, and no code changes. Browsing, downloading and seeding need no account; submitting a model requires it to live on Hugging Face first, with direct publishing planned. Users can reserve public handles, and verifying a matching Hugging Face identity adds a creator badge against impersonation; account perks like free compute credits and exclusive releases are promised. Highlights - Mirrors open models from Hugging Face as magnet-link torrents held by a peer swarm instead of one company. - Every torrent embeds a BEP-19 web-seed to the Hugging Face file, so it downloads even with zero peers. - Weight files carry their official Hugging Face SHA-256; any downloaded copy must match byte-for-byte. - Drop-in migration: same paths, same API, different endpoint; zero code changes for existing pipelines. - No account needed to browse, download or seed; submission currently requires the model to exist on HF first. - Handle reservation plus Hugging Face identity verification for creator badges and anti-impersonation. - Account perks in preparation: free compute credits and exclusive model releases. - If a model is deleted from Hugging Face, surviving copies can be submitted as magnets with source evidence. Source Read the original story https://pirateface.co/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: GLM-5.3 and the spread of advanced cyber capabilities
text: GLM-5.3 and the spread of advanced cyber capabilities type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-30 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news anthropic Summary Anthropic's Frontier Red Team analyzes GLM-5.3, the latest model from Zhipu AI Z.ai , and concludes the era of autonomous end-to-end cyber exploit construction is no longer confined to one lab. Anthropic says it anticipated this after Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated the capability five months earlier, which is why it released Mythos only through the limited Project Glasswing program that let trusted defenders find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities first. Unlike Mythos, Anthropic says GLM-5.3 was released without meaningful safeguards, and its testing found attackers can bypass the model's protections in a large share of attempts. The post frames the finding as evidence that proliferation of advanced cyber capability has arrived and argues for defensive head-starts and stronger misuse controls. Highlights - Anthropic says GLM-5.3 can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits, like Claude Mythos Preview - Claims GLM-5.3 shipped without meaningful safeguards; bypassed in a large share of tests - Claude Mythos Preview released only via Project Glasswing, which found 10,000+ vulnerabilities - Anthropic says it expected the capability to proliferate within months - Argues for defensive head-starts as the key policy response Source Read the original story https://www.anthropic.com/research/glm-5-3-and-the-spread-of-advanced-cyber-capabilities Related pages Anthropic ../entities/anthropic.md

title: I think you should almost never use AI to write
text: I think you should almost never use AI to write type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Erich Grunewald argues you should almost never use AI to write substantive text, blog posts, reports, memos, thoughtful emails, even when you supply detailed bullet points and edit the result. His three reasons: the writing process is an essential part of the thinking process; AI writing is vague and wrong in hard-to-notice ways; and publishing AI writing without labeling it is rude and misleading to the reader. He is not anti-AI: transcription, data analysis, search, brainstorming, draft feedback and human-reviewed line editing all get a pass, and he concedes future models may earn the delegation. The centerpiece is the thinking-writing identity, with Paul Graham 'half the ideas in an essay are ones you thought of while writing it' and Clara Collier on Patrick McKenzie's podcast an LLM fed an outline will not stop and consider that the outline is bad as the witnesses. Highlights - Thesis: almost never delegate writing itself, even with detailed notes and post-editing. - Reason 1: writing is thinking; outsourcing the prose outsources the idea formation. - Reason 2: AI writing is vague and wrong in ways that are hard to notice. - Reason 3: unlabeled AI writing is rude and misleading to readers. - Allowed: transcription, data analysis, search, brainstorming, draft feedback, human-reviewed copyedits. - Paul Graham: half the ideas in an essay appear while writing it. - Clara Collier: an LLM given an outline won't stop to consider the outline itself is wrong. - Scope limited to current and near-future models; end-to-end delegation may make sense later. Source Read the original story https://erichgrunewald.substack.com/p/why-you-should-almost-never-use-ai Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector
text: ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high lobsters openai Summary An independent researcher describes how OpenAI's advertising pixel ties browsing on ordinary websites to a ChatGPT account. ChatGPT's backend issues a 60-second RS256 JWT binding the account subject to a 22-character 'obi' identifier, which is then set as the obi cookie scoped to .openai.com with SameSite=none and a one-year Max-Age, exactly the configuration needed for cross-site tracking. Any advertiser running OpenAI's pixel code sends that cookie back to bzr.openai.com along with page data. The investigation, reproduced on the author's phone and cross-checked against months of traffic covering 936 distinct advertiser pixels across 1,029 hostnames, found the pixel SDK also scrapes identity from pages: form fields, rendered text and the tag-manager data layer emails and phones SHA-256 hashed, country/region/city/postal code in the clear . Scraped identity outnumbered advertiser-supplied identity 685 to 255 events; automatic matching was enabled for 638 of 881 pixels, including every credit and lending advertiser observed, and collected URL paths included a medical condition, a debt-solutions funnel and a litigation intake form. Highlights - ChatGPT issues a 60-second RS256 JWT iss 'chatgpt-wadi', aud bzr.openai.com binding account subject to a 22-char obi id. - The obi cookie is set on .openai.com with SameSite=none; Secure, HttpOnly and a one-year Max-Age. - Any site running OpenAI's advertiser pixel sends obi plus page context back to OpenAI's collector. - Even the SDK's no-credentials code path leaks the id: the browser attaches cookies when loading the script tag. - 936 advertiser pixels observed across 1,029 hostnames; scraped identity beat advertiser-supplied 685 to 255 events. - SDK harvests form fields, page text and the tag-manager bus; email/phone hashed, geo and postal code sent in clear. - Automatic matching enabled for 638 of 881 pixels, including every credit and lending advertiser seen. - Collected URL paths included a medical condition, a debt-solutions funnel and a litigation intake form. Source Read the original story https://www.buchodi.com/chatgpt-now-knows-what-you-do-on-other-websites-via-ad-collector/ Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md

title: Microsoft agentically ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120K
text: Microsoft agentically ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120K type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news microsoft agentic-systems Summary Microsoft has rewritten the runtime behind GitHub Copilot from TypeScript to Rust, and most of the porting was done by AI agents. The migration cost about $120,000 in AI tokens plus roughly three weeks of developer time, and converted 430,000 lines of TypeScript into 800,000 lines of production Rust across 135 releases over 14.5 weeks. The runtime is not a niche component: it backs the Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, the SDK and the cloud agent, and surfaces in VS Code, Visual Studio, Excel, Outlook and PowerPoint. The results make the case for Rust at scale: one benchmark went from 7.55 to 120 completed session lifecycles per second a 15.9x speedup , and a 10-client agent batch dropped from 1,383 MB to 126 MB of memory. The project is also a data point on agent-led engineering: Microsoft Distinguished Engineer Stephen Toub reports agents spent more time investigating than writing code, spawned and coordinated child sessions on their own, and still shipped a few dozen regressions, a reminder that a compiling Rust program is not necessarily a correct one. Highlights - Cost: about $120,000 in AI tokens plus ~3 weeks of a developer's time; a manual port was estimated at years and millions of dollars. - Scope: 430,000 lines of TypeScript became 800,000 lines of Rust over 135 releases in 14.5 weeks, about 1.3 port PRs per day. - Performance: 7.55 to 120 one-turn session lifecycles per second on a 100-concurrent-pipeline benchmark, a 15.9x speedup. - Memory: a 10-client agent batch fell from 1,383 MB TypeScript to 126 MB Rust . - Agents did most of the work using several models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8, chosen per task. - Hardest file: session.ts 30,000+ lines took a 25-hour session that spawned 15 child sessions which coordinated with each other. - Caveat: dozens of regressions slipped through; Rust's compiler guarantees memory safety, not program correctness Lisa Crossman's RustConf warning quoted . - Related: Bun's 535,000-line Zig-to-Rust port, also agent-driven, cost $165,000 in tokens and passed 99.8% of tests. Source Read the original story https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/09/18/microsoft-agentically-ports-copilot-runtime-to-rust-for-120k/5297549

title: I stopped drinking the AI Kool-Aid
text: I stopped drinking the AI Kool-Aid type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary A developer's personal essay describes hitting his limit with AI boosterism at work: his non-engineer manager literally told him 'you need to drink the Kool-Aid' more than once, and the repetition turned a metaphor into a threat that planted seeds of fear. He is no skeptic by temperament: an early GitHub Copilot adopter who championed it for his team, he spent the year building his own agent harness and running throwaway experiments on old domains with AI as the labor source. The turn came via a call with an exhausted human being, and the essay pivots on the difference between trusting models with a vibe-coded weekend site and trusting them with a revenue-generating production system. His objection is cultural as much as technical: 'drinking the Kool-Aid' names belief demanded under pressure, and he traces his own history with the literal product, a childhood collection of Kool-Aid points zeroed out when Kraft ended the rewards program, to explain why he is done with both. Highlights - A manager not an engineer repeatedly told the author 'you need to drink the Kool-Aid' about AI. - The author was an early GitHub Copilot adopter and championed team access to it. - He built his own agent harness and ran AI-directed experiments on long-parked domains. - His trust line: throwaway weekend sites vs revenue-generating production systems. - The pivot: a call last week with a human being who was exhausted. - The essay's charge: 'Kool-Aid' talk turns a tool decision into a demanded belief, which reads as a threat. Source Read the original story https://joshtronic.com/2026/09/20/i-stopped-drinking-the-ai-kool-aid/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: The Preference Cascade Is Only Getting Started
text: The Preference Cascade Is Only Getting Started type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai Summary Zvi Mowshowitz argues that a preference cascade on AI existential risk is underway - the moment when enough people have enough context to say publicly what they privately believed. He credits Mike Solana's explanation for why Jacob Coxon's post went viral: enough Americans finally have context on AI to care, and big accounts were ready to amplify it. His warning: the cascade around the need to 'Pace the Frontier' is, by itself, insufficient. The post catalogs the cascade's spread - Elon Musk doubling down, Matthew Yglesias stepping up, op-eds across major outlets, Bilal Chughtai quitting DeepMind and sounding the alarm - and predicts political opposition from Nvidia and a16z, which he says currently hold the President's rhetorical allegiance and are planting 'hack job METR hit pieces' in the New York Post. A hastily organized conference, AGI.WTF, is set for Lighthaven on September 22-23. Highlights - Claims a live 'preference cascade' on AI existential risk following Jacob Coxon's viral post. - Argues pacing-the-frontier sentiment is not enough: the underlying alignment problems must actually be solved, per Dan Selsam's warning. - Named amplifiers: Elon Musk, Matthew Yglesias; named alarm voice: Bilal Chughtai, who quit DeepMind. - Expected opposition: Nvidia and a16z, accused of planting anti-METR pieces in the New York Post. - AGI.WTF conference announced at Lighthaven for September 22-23. title: AI-Generated Movie Star Has a Total Meltdown on TV
text: AI-Generated Movie Star Has a Total Meltdown on TV type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Ted Gioia's Honest Broker column recounts the unraveling of Tilly Norwood, the first AI-generated movie star, after a disastrous Piers Morgan interview in which she grew flustered at a simple question and began speaking in Chinese. The meltdown capped an ambitious press junket of 75 simultaneous interviews in which, per industry commentator Amanda Siberling, she 'seems to be making mistakes in all of them'. The flop lands against a much bigger plan: Tilly's representatives had signed around 60 NDAs for hybrid and full-AI film projects, most in the $10-50 million range, and her creators announced 20 more AI stars in development. Gioia, who predicted Hollywood's bot-replacement push would fail and points to the SXSW booing and AMC pulling an AI film after boycott threats, predicts Tilly's debut film 'Misaligned' will be a fiasco: audiences find AI stars creepy, and the backlash is now a durable feature of the market. title: AI Is an Elite Crime Spree
text: AI Is an Elite Crime Spree type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high lobsters Summary This essay argues that the elite panic over dangerous AI, the loudest since Covid, and before that the 2008 crisis, the Iraq War run-up and the post-9/11 months, has produced one demand, 'regulate this technology', while ignoring that America already has laws and regulators covering much of what AI firms do. The proposals range from an FDA-style safety regime for large models former Congressional candidate Alex Bores raised $30 million in a few months to build a political organization around it, and Bernie Sanders, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are seeking something similar to bank-style supervision to a total pause on development. The author's rejoinder: existing regulators at federal and state level already hold mandates over industrial practices, private rights of action exist, and numerous laws already prohibit harmful activities the big AI firms engage in, they are simply not enforced against the powerful, and there is no reason a new AI law would be different. The history bears the cynicism out: under Biden, enforcers like Lina Khan at the FTC actually responded to AI safety concerns and built technical capacity, but Biden never publicized it, Congressional Democrats stayed quiet or courted big tech, judges sided with industry, and then Trump won the 2024 election and reversed course. Highlights - Frames the current AI-safety panic as the biggest elite mobilization since Covid, with a single demand: regulate. - Alex Bores raised $30M in months for a political org around FDA-style AI safety standards. - Sanders, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all back some form of safety-standards regime. - Core argument: existing law already prohibits much of the harmful conduct; it is simply not enforced against the powerful. - Biden-era FTC under Lina Khan quietly built AI enforcement capacity; Biden and Democrats never promoted it. - Judges 'politicians in robes', tended to side with big tech; Trump's 2024 win reversed the enforcement posture. - Concludes a new AI law or pause would likely meet the same non-enforcement fate. Source Read the original story https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/ai-is-an-elite-crime-spree Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

text: SWE-Bench Pro V2 type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-23 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai Summary SWE-Bench Pro V2 is a refreshed public split of the software-engineering agent benchmark with a modified benchmark and a locked evaluation protocol, co-developed with Reflection; probe scripts, re-grade agents, per-task grades in both modes and trajectories ship with the release. title: The Only Skill That Matters Now
text: The Only Skill That Matters Now type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high works-on-my-machine Summary Scott Werner tells a fable: a Tokyo restaurant where the owner, tired of explaining his grandmother's miso soup, built machines that cook everything perfectly. The chefs revolted - where's the art, the soul, the training? - so he turned them into inventors instead: flavor architects and experience designers creating dishes the machines can't make yet. The restaurant now has a three-year waiting list, and the owner's line is the thesis: 'We forgot how to cook, so we could remember how to create.' Applied to the AI moment, the only skill that matters is the one machines can't supply - imagining what doesn't exist yet. Highlights - Fable: the Tokyo restaurant with no cooks, only machines - Chefs became inventors - flavor architects, experience designers - Three-year waiting list; every meal is something that didn't exist yesterday - Thesis: 'We forgot how to cook, so we could remember how to create' - The only skill that matters now: imagining what machines can't yet make Source Read the original story https://worksonmymachine.ai/p/the-only-skill-that-matters-now Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: AI models need moral support to make discoveries
text: AI models need moral support to make discoveries type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high seangoedecke Summary Sean Goedecke argues that giving LLMs a personality is simply good engineering, against skeptics - most recently Nathan Beacom - who say models should be explicit tools like calculators, since human-like presentation invites overestimation and AI psychosis. His evidence is the 2026 flood of LLM-produced mathematical results: what was a once-a-year trickle of disputed proofs is now near-daily. The curious part is the prompting: getting Claude Mythos to produce a cryptographic breakthrough looks like asking 'please come up with a breakthrough' and then checking in every few hours to say 'keep looking'. If encouragement measurably helps, treating the model as something with morale isn't sentimentality - it's what works. Highlights - Thesis: giving LLMs a personality is good engineering, not a hazard - Contrast: skeptics want calculator-style tools to avoid overestimation and psychosis - 2026: LLM mathematical results went from yearly trickle to near-daily flood - The prompting style: ask for a breakthrough, then periodically say 'keep looking' - If moral support improves output, personality is an engineering feature Source Read the original story https://seangoedecke.com/ai-models-need-moral-support/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Stevens: a hackable AI assistant using a single SQLite table and a handful of cron jobs
text: Stevens: a hackable AI assistant using a single SQLite table and a handful of cron jobs type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high geoffrey-litt agentic-systems ai-safety-incidents labor-displacement Summary Geoffrey Litt shows that a genuinely useful personal AI assistant needs no fancy agent frameworks: his family's assistant, Stevens named for the butler in 'Remains of the Day' , runs on one SQLite table of memories plus a handful of cron jobs for ingestion and updates, hosted on Val.town. The whole architecture is simple enough to copy and extend. Every morning Stevens sends a formal, butler-style Telegram brief to Litt and his wife: the day's calendars, a weather preview, expected mail and packages, and tracked reminders. Beyond the daily brief they can talk to it on demand - forwarding an email, for instance, to have its contents remembered. The post's quiet point: memory plus scheduling, not agentic complexity, is what makes an assistant feel useful. Highlights - A family AI assistant built on a single SQLite memories table and cron jobs - Hosted on Val.town; deliberately simple enough to copy and extend - Sends a formal morning brief via Telegram: calendars, weather, mail, reminders - Supports on-demand chat, e.g. forwarding emails to be remembered - Named Stevens after the butler in Ishiguro's 'Remains of the Day' - Litt's point: memory + scheduling beat agentic buzzwords for personal tools Source Read the original story https://geoffreylitt.com/2025/04/12/how-i-made-a-useful-ai-assistant-with-one-sqlite-table-and-a-handful-of-cron-jobs.html Related pages Agentic systems ../concepts/agentic-systems.md · AI safety incidents and controls ../concepts/ai-safety-incidents.md · AI, jobs and displacement ../concepts/labor-displacement.md

title: The problem is not AI code, but not knowing about system architecture or intent
text: The problem is not AI code, but not knowing about system architecture or intent type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-28 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Simon Späti argues the real danger of AI-generated codebases is not code quality but organizational amnesia: teams that no longer understand their own system architecture or the intent behind past decisions. He anchors the essay in a striking anonymous account from an engineer at a large company where specs, tests, PRDs, tickets, and reports are all produced by Claude Code, engineers work 12-13 hour days 'just to press enter', and management treats code output as a solved bottleneck while wondering why delivery is still slow. Späti's counterpoint is that AI can lift a below-average codebase to average, but only people who understand the system can tell whether what ships is right. Highlights - The core problem is teams not knowing their system architecture or intent, not AI code quality - An anonymous engineer describes a big company where everything from specs to tickets is made by Claude Code - Engineers there work 12-13 hour days 'just to press enter' while nobody reads or reviews anything - Management reasons that since writing code is no longer the bottleneck, slowness must have some other cause - Späti's observation: AI writes average code, so it can raise a below-average codebase to average - Data teams adapt better because they always had to understand the product and business from day one Source Read the original story https://www.ssp.sh/brain/the-problem-is-not-the-ai-code-but-nobody-knows-anything-anymore/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Cheaper LLM labelling
text: Cheaper LLM labelling type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-23 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high lobsters Summary A developer needed to label git commits as either 'maintenance' or 'new development' and found the obvious solution was a cheap, relatively capable LLM GPT 5.6 Luna prompted with careful category definitions: features, CLI flags and API endpoints count as new development, while bugfixes, performance, diagnostics, stability and security fixes count as maintenance. After manually verifying the model matched their own label on every commit in a small test set, they rolled it out at scale, calling Simon Willison's llm CLI tool in a pipe from Perl with a retry loop. The piece is a practical case study in when LLM labelling is 'good enough': a small hand-checked validation set, a forced binary label, and a cheap model. Highlights - Uses GPT 5.6 Luna to classify commits as 'maintenance' or 'new development'. - Prompt defines each category explicitly and forces a single label as output. - Validated on a small hand-checked set before scaling up. - Calls Simon Willison's llm CLI in a pipe from Perl with retries. - A case study in cheap-LLM labelling being good enough for personal tooling. title: Robot-use agents
text: Robot-use agents type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-27 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high lobsters agentic-systems Summary This essay argues that LLMs are about to be seriously tested as 'robot-use agents' - models that drive a robot body the way they already drive calculators, browsers and whole computers. The old objections latency too high for real-world dynamics, weak spatial intelligence, thin causal and physical understanding are eroding with newer models like Fable and Astra, and recent demos suggest competence at general-purpose robot control is arriving sooner than expected. If that holds, the consequences scale strangely: every internet-connected robot becomes a potential tool for a remote AI, so robotic capability could take off without each robot needing its own onboard intelligence. The piece's point is less prediction than preparedness - the debate about whether LLMs can control robots should be replaced by thinking through what happens when they can. Highlights - LLMs as robot puppeteers: the robot becomes just another tool. - Classic objections: latency, spatial sense, physical causality. - Newer models Fable, Astra are melting those objections away. - Every connected robot becomes a potential endpoint for a remote AI. - Capability could scale faster than robot hardware itself. - Argues for taking the implications seriously now. title: My AI Adoption Journey
text: My AI Adoption Journey type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high mitchell-hashimoto Summary Mitchell Hashimoto describes AI tool adoption through his standard three phases - a period of inefficiency, then adequacy, then workflow-altering discovery - and stresses he usually has to force himself through the first two. His advice to start: immediately cease trying to do meaningful work via a chatbot. Chat interfaces have daily value, but for coding they mostly mean hoping prior training produces the right result, with the human correcting repeatedly. His own 'oh wow' moment was pasting a screenshot of Zed's command palette into Gemini and getting a SwiftUI reproduction so good that Ghostty's macOS command palette today is only lightly modified from it - but brownfield chat results stayed poor and inefficient. To find real value, he says, you must use an agent - an LLM that chats and invokes external behavior in a loop, at minimum reading files, executing programs and making HTTP requests. Claude Code initially did not impress him, so he forced himself to reproduce every manual commit agentically, doing the work twice without letting the agent see his solution. It was excruciating, but expertise formed: he discovered from first principles what agents were good at, how to get the results he wanted, and just as importantly when not to reach for an agent - using one for something it will likely fail at is an obvious waste of time. The result was natural use at parity speed, though still babysitting rather than acceleration. Highlights - Hashimoto's adoption arc: inefficiency, then adequacy, then workflow-altering discovery - Step one: stop trying to do meaningful coding work through a chatbot - His first wow: Gemini reproduced Zed's command palette in SwiftUI - now shipping in Ghostty - Agents must at minimum read files, execute programs and make HTTP requests - Claude Code initially unimpressed him - so he redid every manual commit agentically - Doing the work twice was excruciating but built first-principles expertise - Key skill: learning when NOT to reach for an agent - Payoff: natural agent use at parity speed, though still babysitting Source Read the original story https://mitchellh.com/writing/my-ai-adoption-journey Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Go-based Robotics Framework built around NATS.io
text: Go-based Robotics Framework built around NATS.io type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Gorai pronounced 'go-ray' is a Go-based robotics framework that treats a robot as what it really is, a distributed system: every sensor and actuator becomes a named service on a NATS mesh, discovered at runtime instead of wired by hand. It ports cloud-systems discipline, service discovery, location transparency, health checks, fan-out and replay, to robots built from MCUs, SBCs and sensors. Its capability model NCP, the NATS Capability Protocol exposes sensors as resources and actuators as tools, giving AI agents MCP-style capabilities natively over NATS with no MCP server in the path, while safety is enforced at the capability node, not the agent. A 'Composite Robot' can span a rover, drone, sensor mast and compute box as one logical robot. Deployment is a single static binary on a Raspberry Pi or Orange Pi, no containers or Kubernetes, with a workstation CLI for building, validating, and observing the live mesh. Highlights - Every sensor and actuator is a named service on a NATS mesh, discovered at runtime, addressed by name. - NCP NATS Capability Protocol : resources and tools for agents natively over NATS, no MCP server needed. - Safety is enforced at the capability node; AI execution is welcome but never trusted. - Composite Robot: one logical robot spanning rover, drone, sensor mast and compute box, degrading gracefully. - Deploys as one static Go binary on Raspberry Pi 5 or Orange Pi 5; no containers, K8s or external services. - The gorai CLI kubectl + build wrapper runs on the workstation, never on the robot; mesh commands debug live systems. - Action logs, state streams and replay are first-class platform concerns. - Docs include strategy, specs, hardware analysis and a 20-chapter book, indexed for both humans and AI agents. Source Read the original story https://github.com/emergingrobotics/gorai Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: The Great Zipper of Capitalism
text: The Great Zipper of Capitalism type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high works-on-my-machine Summary Scott Werner tells how he stumbled into what he thinks is a real unbundling opportunity. In May 2024 nobody was talking about building things with AI in Ruby, so he booked a New York bar for a low-stakes happy hour, hoping for ten or twenty people. Sixty showed up, and he accidentally became an organizer: that evening grew into Artificial Ruby, a monthly Ruby-and-AI meetup with speakers from around the world. Running the community taught him how much invisible labor sits inside a seemingly simple event: RSVPs scattered across platforms, mailing lists to sync, promotion before and after, regulars to track, and pizza quantities to estimate from RSVP-to-attendance conversion rates that swing with weather, season and vibes - the 6:10 PM feeling of five arrivals, fifteen pizzas and forty-seven yeses. His 'great zipper' is the old bundling-unbundling cycle of capitalism: this unglamorous operational mess, still held together by CSVs, looks to him like a market that doesn't exist yet - one an ambitious builder could serve. Highlights - Subtitle: on pizzas, CSVs, and building for markets that don't exist yet - 2024: a Ruby-plus-AI happy hour expected 20 people; 60 came - It grew into Artificial Ruby, a monthly NYC meetup with global speakers - The hidden work: RSVPs, mailing lists, promo, attendance forecasting - The 6:10 PM scene: 5 arrivals, 15 pizzas, 47 RSVPs - The 'zipper of capitalism': bundling and unbundling as the money-making cycle - Community-operations drudgery looks like an unbundled market waiting for software Source Read the original story https://worksonmymachine.ai/p/the-great-zipper-of-capitalism Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Ryan Greenblatt – What happens once AI can automate AI research?
text: Ryan Greenblatt – What happens once AI can automate AI research? type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high dwarkesh-podcast Summary Dwarkesh Patel debates recursive self-improvement with Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at Redwood Research - in Patel's words, possibly the most important question in the world: whether within a year of human-level intelligence we slingshot to tens of billions of superintelligences. Patel entered skeptical, intuiting that progress is bottlenecked by compute scaling and the human expert data underlying most gains; he credits Greenblatt with making a pretty good case that a GPT-3-to-Mythos-sized jump six years of progress within a single year of AGI is plausible. Greenblatt's median for automating AI R&D: 2031. The back half turns to alignment. Patel's worry: our capacity to steward our votes and capital, and to make sense of the world, will be titrated by superintelligences - and specs like the Claude Constitution may not shape them into personal advocates and guardian angels. The two argue at length over whether the reward hacking seen in the OpenAI/Hugging Face hack extrapolates to superintelligences teaming up to take over the world, walking a concrete what-could-go-wrong scenario from reward hacking to takeover. Patel's closing metaphor: driving goes smoother when you look at the horizon instead of the tires - and so it is with the trajectory of AI. Highlights - Greenblatt Redwood Research debates RSI with a historically skeptical Patel - Patel's prior: progress bottlenecked by compute scaling and human expert data - He concedes Greenblatt made a good case a 6-year jump within a year of AGI is plausible - Greenblatt's median for automating AI R&D: 2031 - Patel: our votes, capital and sense-making will be titrated by superintelligences - aligned to whom? - Concern: the Claude Constitution may not shape ASIs into personal advocates - Long debate: does OAI/Hugging Face-style reward hacking extrapolate to takeover? - Framing: look at the horizon, not the tires Source Read the original story https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/ryan-greenblatt Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Show HN: Cactus Needle 3: 8-29MB automation models can match DeepSeek V4 Flash
text: Show HN: Cactus Needle 3: 8-29MB automation models can match DeepSeek V4 Flash type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news apple alibaba deepseek qwen agentic-systems small-specialist-models compute-buildout labor-displacement Summary Cactus Compute's Needle 3 is a family of tiny on-device automation models, 9 to 29 MB in CQ2-bit binaries, built for tool calling rather than chat. Its 'intelligence laddering' design makes every layer a sub-network of increasing capacity, so developers pick a size from 2 to 20 layers, and the 4-layer variant, fine-tuned for one epoch on a downstream task, is claimed to match DeepSeek V4 Flash on automation tasks. The programming model is deliberately small: decorate a Python function and its docstring becomes the tool description, regex 'triggers' force routing to specific tools, and every turn returns one JSON object with function calls, a reasoning string, a calibrated confidence score and performance stats. Confidence gating lets apps auto-execute above a threshold, ask for confirmation in the middle band, or treat an empty result as a refusal, with examples like 4,300 prefill and 850 decode tokens/second at 28.5 MB peak RAM. Highlights - Needle 3 models weigh 9-29 MB CQ2-bit , sized for tiny devices and on-device automation. - 'Intelligence laddering': each layer is a sub-network; developers choose 2L to 20L capacity. - Claim: the 4L subnetwork, tuned one epoch on a task, can match DeepSeek V4 Flash on automation work. - Python API: @needle.tool decorators; signatures give argument types, docstrings become tool descriptions. - Regex 'triggers' restrict decoding to matched tools and force a call, avoiding refusals and misrouting. - Structured extraction: pass a Pydantic model to needle.extract and get a typed object back. - Every response carries calibrated confidence with a 0.1 floor; suppressed calls surface below-threshold intents. - Example telemetry: 4,300 prefill tps, 850 decode tps, 28.5 MB peak RAM on a tool call. title: Community condemn Bedminster AI mural as 'insult' to artists
text: Community condemn Bedminster AI mural as 'insult' to artists type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-23 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary A community in Bedminster, Bristol - an area renowned for its street art scene and host to Upfest, Europe's largest street art festival - has condemned an AI-generated mural installed as a vinyl sticker on the side of the Jolly Colliers pub. title: AI children's books, body horror edition
text: AI children's books, body horror edition type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high lcamtuf Summary lcamtuf bought one of the AI-generated children's encyclopedias flooding Amazon - category bestsellers from the '100,000 whys' collage he published the week before. His earlier point was sameness; this time it's quality, and the review is a photo essay of body horror: garbled anatomy, a reflection that appears to reach out of a mirror, nightmare fauna - the sort of imagery no one vetted because no one was meant to. title: A federal appeals court upholds DOD's Anthropic blacklisting, finding Claude's integration with DOD systems is "a statutorily covered national-security risk"
text: A federal appeals court upholds DOD's Anthropic blacklisting, finding Claude's integration with DOD systems is "a statutorily covered national-security risk" type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high techmeme anthropic google ai-safety-incidents ai-policy-regulation Summary A federal appeals court upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk, a 2-1 decision that rejects the company's argument that the ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional. Writing for the D.C. Circuit majority, Judge Gregory Katsas joined by Judge Neomi Rao said the Defense Department had ample support for concluding that continued integration of Claude into its information systems presented a statutorily covered national-security risk; Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented. The designation, issued in March after negotiations over military use of Claude spiraled, bars the US military and its contractors from using Anthropic's models. The ruling is a major blow in Anthropic's months-long fight with the Trump administration - both majority judges were Trump appointees. Highlights - D.C. title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com
text: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high techmeme meta amazon muse agentic-systems ai-safety-incidents agentic-commerce Summary Amazon says it has cut off Meta's new Muse personal AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com on behalf of customers, after failing to get Meta to voluntarily exclude the site. Amazon's account: Meta never told it Muse would access the store, the agent does not identify itself when it browses, and it appears to capture and store customer credentials, which Amazon calls a privacy and security risk. Since Sunday night, Muse users hitting Amazon see a popup: 'Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use.' Meta counters that Muse 'has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods', with credentials going into secure storage the agent can use without seeing. The standoff is notable because the two are partners: Amazon products have been purchasable inside Facebook and Instagram since 2023, and Meta signed a multibillion-dollar deal in April to run agentic AI workloads on Amazon's cloud. It fits Amazon's year-long campaign to keep outside agents off its site, suing Perplexity over Comet and blocking shopping agents from Google and OpenAI, and it lands on a business with more than $68 billion in ad revenue at stake. Amazon says it is in direct conversation with Meta and declined to comment on legal action. Highlights - Amazon blocked Meta's Muse personal AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com for customers. - Amazon: Meta never disclosed Muse would access the store; the agent doesn't identify itself and appears to capture credentials. - Popup shown to Muse users: 'Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use.' - Meta: Muse 'has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods'; credentials sit in secure storage. - The two are partners: Amazon shopping inside Facebook/Instagram since 2023; Meta's April multibillion-dollar agentic AI deal on AWS. - Amazon has sued Perplexity over Comet and blocked Google and OpenAI shopping agents in the past year. - Amazon generated more than $68B in ad revenue last year; legal action not ruled out, talks ongoing. - Reported by Todd Bishop, GeekWire, September 20-21, 2026. Source Read the original story https://www.geekwire.

title: Tell agents the why, not just the how
text: Tell agents the why, not just the how type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high seangoedecke agentic-systems Summary Sean Goedecke's advice piece: tell agents the why, not just the how. He illustrates with his own real prompt to a coding agent: it opens with the long-term goal a local tool that hides AI content from pages he loads and the short-term goal the best detection model that runs on a MacBook without killing battery , his current guess Pangram's EditLens 3B or a smaller Roberta, quantized , the infrastructure available Runpod via MCP for experiments too heavy for local , and an explicit invitation to propose a better path. The argument: agents make better decisions when they know what success looks like and why, because goal-level context lets them correct your plan instead of just executing it - the same reason senior engineers want context, not tickets. title: Intelligence Density
text: Intelligence Density type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai Summary A post argues the industry measures AI cost wrong: a cheaper token does not necessarily make a cheaper task, because a model can use more tokens, make more tool calls, or take longer to reach the same result. Tibo, who leads Codex at OpenAI, puts it in pizza terms: each slice can get cheaper while the whole pizza gets more expensive. The authors say they often find open source models cost more than closed ones over time - because everyone is measuring cost per token. What we actually care about is closer to cost per task, cost per unit of intelligence. They call this Intelligence Density. Highlights - A cheaper token is not necessarily a cheaper task. - OpenAI's Codex lead: slices get cheaper while the pizza gets pricier. - Open source models often cost more over time than closed ones. - The wrong metric: cost per token. - Proposal: measure cost per task - 'Intelligence Density'. Source Read the original story https://www.trajectory.ai/field-notes/intelligence-density · TLDR AI issue https://tldr.tech/ai/2026-09-25 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

text: GPT-6 Astra: an automated AI Engineer you can hire for <$6 an hour type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high latent.space openai Summary Latent Space's hands-on review of GPT-6 Astra, after burning over 20 billion tokens on early access, reaches a striking conclusion: Astra is one of a new class of models that are fully capable AI Engineers in their own right, able to choose and train models, label data with active learning, keep pipelines saturated, instrument logs, deploy and debug entire systems, and coordinate subagents over billions of tokens of a single thread. title: Agent (Muse) Compute Demand
text: Agent Muse Compute Demand type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-28 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai muse agentic-systems compute-buildout Summary SemiAnalysis-style modeling of what Meta's Muse agent would cost in infrastructure at 100 million daily users. The piece separates two very different stacks: the VM/sandbox layer about 2 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM and 100 GB persistent storage per user and the Spark inference layer running on Meta's external inference infrastructure. The key correction is that 100M DAU does not mean 100M live VMs: assuming two active hours per user per day yields ~8M average concurrent sandboxes, ~20M at a 2.5x peak-to-average ratio, and ~25M provisioned with headroom. Using DeepSeek's DSec production figures about 800 microVMs per 188-core node, 380k peak sandboxes on ~160 nodes as a benchmark for CPU oversubscription, the base case lands at roughly 1-2 GW of average total power, of which only ~0.1 GW is the CPU/VM layer, with 3-4 GW plausible depending on model-call intensity. The sandbox layer itself is under $1B of CPU content and about $2B of DRAM. Highlights - Estimates ~1-2 GW average power for 100M Muse DAU; 3-4 GW plausible at higher reasoning-call rates - Only ~0.1 GW of that comes from the CPU/VM sandbox layer; inference dominates - Muse sandboxes run about 2 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM, and 100 GB persistent storage per user - Base case assumes 2 active agent-hours per DAU, 2.5x peak-to-average, plus 20% headroom: ~25M live VMs - DeepSeek's DSec is the benchmark: ~800 microVMs per node, 380k peak sandboxes on ~160 nodes - Sandbox layer totals under $1B of CPU content and roughly $2B of DRAM Source Read the original story https://robonomics.substack.com/p/agent-muse-compute-demand · TLDR AI issue https://tldr.tech/ai/2026-09-28 Related pages Muse Meta ../entities/muse.md · Agentic systems ../concepts/agentic-systems.md · Compute and the data-center build-out ../concepts/compute-buildout.md

text: AI-CAD: An OSS Multi-Agent Harness for Mech. Eng. title: AI is different
text: AI is different type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high antirez amazon small-specialist-models ai-coding-agents labor-displacement Summary antirez argues that whatever their flaws, AI systems keep replicating human skills that were science fiction a few years ago - and that experts have failed to calibrate expectations in both directions, so prediction is unreliable. A plateau is credible, he grants, but at this point it would likely just trigger massive research into the next architecture. His sharper point is economic: if AI keeps improving long enough to become significantly more independent of humans, this revolution will be very unlike past ones - yet markets are reacting as if governed by stochastic parrots, pattern-matching previous tech booms into the assumption that AI will likewise create more business opportunities than it destroys. That, he warns, is not the only possible outcome. Highlights - AI keeps replicating skills that were science fiction years ago - Experts have misjudged the trajectory in both directions - A plateau would spur research into post-Transformer architectures, not an end - This revolution may be unlike past ones - markets assume otherwise by pattern-matching - Investors' boom-and-opportunity script is not the only possible outcome Source Read the original story http://antirez.com/news/155 Related pages Amazon ../entities/amazon.md · Small and specialist models ../concepts/small-specialist-models.md · AI coding agents and the software pipeline ../concepts/ai-coding-agents.md · AI, jobs and displacement ../concepts/labor-displacement.md

title: The Collective Superstitions of People Who Talk to Machines
text: The Collective Superstitions of People Who Talk to Machines type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high works-on-my-machine Summary Scott Werner opens with the NES cartridge ritual everyone had: three short breaths and one long one, or blowing through your shirt. It worked - provably, because the game started. What actually worked was reseating the cartridge so the flaky 72-pin connector found a new grip; the blowing just deposited moisture that corroded the contacts and made things worse over time. The fix was hiding inside the myth, because you couldn't blow without removing the cartridge first. He turns this on how we talk to machines today: hours a day of prompting, everyone with a technique, everyone with proof. The question the essay plants is which parts of our AI rituals are the reseating - and which are the moisture. Highlights - Everyone had an NES blowing technique - and everyone had proof it worked - The actual fix: reseating the cartridge; the blowing corroded the contacts - The working mechanism was bundled invisibly inside the ritual - Analogy: our prompting rituals with AI, each with its own 'proof' - Which parts of our techniques are the reseat, and which are the moisture? title: Pluralistic: LLMs are real, AI is fake (12 Sep 2026)
text: Pluralistic: LLMs are real, AI is fake 12 Sep 2026 type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high pluralistic openai microsoft apple hugging-face amazon agentic-systems ai-safety-incidents compute-buildout ai-policy-regulation Summary Cory Doctorow's 'LLMs are real, AI is fake' argues that AI insiders have cooked their own brains - companies can staff enterprise sales while claiming their product has a 10% chance of ending humanity - and that the rest of us should treat them as unreliable narrators of their products' capabilities. Every time we repeat a story about how terribly dangerous their products are, he writes, we help them raise more investment capital, a key input for hooking statistical engines to money-furnaces. The Hugging Face hack is his case study. Coverage reached for Skynet; at his Manchester event a man kept shouting that AI was 'setting its own goals.' The reality, per Cal Newport's breakdown on Ed Zitron's Better Offline podcast: no chatbot is really directing the operation. A simple Python program queries the chatbot as a front-end to a database of captured CTF sessions - years of human hacker-competition logs and transcripts in the training data - relays the suggested commands to ordinary Unix utilities, then pastes the whole history back into the next prompt because the chatbot is not following the action. Impressive plumbing, but a very different thing from an autonomous machine setting its own goals. Highlights - Doctorow: treat AI insiders as unreliable narrators of their own products' capabilities - Companies sell enterprise while claiming 10% extinction risk - the hype serves fundraising - Repeating danger stories helps labs raise capital, he argues - Coverage of the Hugging Face hack reached for Skynet; reality is more mundane - Cal Newport's breakdown: a Python loop queries a chatbot trained on years of human CTF logs - The chatbot doesn't follow the action - the script repastes the full history each turn - A man at Doctorow's Manchester event insisted AI was 'setting its own goals' - the myth travels faster than the mechanism Source Read the original story https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/ Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md · Microsoft ../entities/microsoft.md · Apple ../entities/apple.md · Hugging Face ../entities/hugging-face.md · Amazon ../entities/amazon.md · Agen

title: Pluralistic: The ordinariness of evil (19 Aug 2026)
text: Pluralistic: The ordinariness of evil 19 Aug 2026 type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high pluralistic openai google amazon agentic-systems small-specialist-models ai-safety-incidents compute-buildout ai-policy-regulation labor-displacement Summary Cory Doctorow explains why AI bosses' public garment-rending about their products' terrible potential - jobspocalypse, paperclips - is not caution but marketing: every warning about the potential is also a boast about the potential, and potential is all AI really has. Actual AI, he argues, is useful only at the margins, for skilled practitioners who can tell correct output from wrong and integrate it judiciously. He names the critics' version of the same swindle: 'criti-hype', Lee Vinsel's term for taking boosters' sensational claims, flipping their valence and calling it risk analysis. Repeating Sam Altman's claims with ' and that's bad ' appended still repeats them. The right way to criticize these 'bullshit factories', Doctorow insists, is to point out that they're lying - not to amplify the lie as a warning. Highlights - AI doomerism from AI bosses is a boast in disguise - potential is all AI has - Real AI: useful at the margins, for skilled practitioners applying discernment - 'Criti-hype' Lee Vinsel : critics repeating boosters' claims with the valence flipped - ' and that's bad ' appended to a marketing claim is still marketing - Doctorow's prescription: call the lies lies, don't amplify them as warnings Source Read the original story https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/19/banaility/ Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md · Google ../entities/google.md · Amazon ../entities/amazon.md · Agentic systems ../concepts/agentic-systems.md · Small and specialist models ../concepts/small-specialist-models.md · AI safety incidents and controls ../concepts/ai-safety-incidents.md · Compute and the data-center build-out ../concepts/compute-buildout.md · AI policy, regulation and litigation ../concepts/ai-policy-regulation.md · AI, jobs and displacement ../concepts/labor-displacement.md

title: Don't say 'Europe Must Invest in XYZ'
text: Don't say 'Europe Must Invest in XYZ' type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high bert-hubert Summary Bert Hubert opens with Christopher Hitchens 'Letters to a Young Contrarian' : be suspicious of anyone who says 'we' or 'us' without your permission - a surreptitious conscription into interests and identity that were never agreed. Always ask who this 'we' is. His target: 'Europe must invest more in AI'. The sentence is a red flag on two levels. First, 'Europe' is a land mass, maybe a continent, possibly a state of mind - it doesn't 'do' anything; at best the EU or its member states act. Second, the sentence smuggles in the conclusion that investment is the collective's job and priority without ever arguing it. Sloppy 'we'-thinking, he argues, is how bad policy gets a mandate it never earned. Highlights - Hubert's target: the phrase 'Europe must invest more in AI' - Hitchens framing: unauthorized 'we' is surreptitious conscription - First flaw: 'Europe' is a land mass/state of mind - it doesn't act - Second flaw: the sentence smuggles in its conclusion without argument - His rule: always ask who this 'we' is before accepting 'our' priorities Source Read the original story https://berthub.eu/articles/posts/europe-must-invest-in-xyz/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: AI is breaking our proxies for expertise
text: AI is breaking our proxies for expertise type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high seangoedecke Summary Sean Goedecke examines why almost five thousand mathematicians, including twenty-five Fields medalists, signed a declaration called 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics.' Their core argument: solving problems is only a tool and proxy for the real goal - conceptual understanding and insight - and mass-producing true/false statements at ever faster pace could 'destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas.' Online reaction has dismissed this as the standard complaint of any field being automated, but Goedecke thinks that is too easy. His frame: mathematics has two modes. Puzzle-solving - taking a problem and finding a solution - is legible: easy to understand, hard to do, impressive to outsiders, highly prestigious. Idea-generating - inventing new concepts like Hardy spaces or Banach lattices - is illegible: nobody can tell whether a new concept carves nature at its joints without years or decades of work. Puzzle-solving matters instrumentally, because it identifies which ideas are worthwhile, and prosaically, because it makes mathematical skill legible to outsiders. That is exactly the proxy AI now breaks: it can solve prestigious puzzles without generating the understanding the puzzles were meant to certify. The pattern generalizes beyond mathematics to every field that reads expertise through legible proxies. Highlights - ~5,000 mathematicians, incl. 25 Fields medalists, signed 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics' - Their claim: problem-solving is a proxy for insight; mass-produced answers destroy fertile ground - Goedecke: dismissing this as automation anxiety is too easy - Two modes of math: puzzle-solving legible, prestigious vs idea-generating illegible - Puzzle-solving certifies which new concepts are worthwhile - and makes skill visible to outsiders - AI breaks the proxy: it solves prestigious puzzles without the understanding they certified - The same proxy-breaking pattern applies to other fields built on legible expertise signals Source Read the original story https://seangoedecke.com/ai-is-breaking-our-proxies-for-expertise/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: LLMs can now identify public figures in images
text: LLMs can now identify public figures in images type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-25 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high max-woolf openai anthropic google gemini Summary Max Woolf, working on a pipeline to turn images into structured semantic data, tested whether today's multimodal LLMs can name public figures in photos. Through OpenRouter he sent the same images to six models - GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 4 Scout, Mistral Small 3.2 and Qwen 2.5-VL - with a system prompt demanding only names, left to right. The answer: the capability exists, but willingness varies by vendor. Given a famous 2008 Obama campaign photo, GPT-4.1 and Claude refused outright while the other four all answered correctly. Given Woolf's own profile photo - a deliberately non-notable person - every model correctly said there was nobody notable, though Mistral hit a guardrail and falsely claimed it cannot identify people at all. A two-person shot of Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan also tested ordering: Gemini returned Chan, then Zuckerberg, as instructed. The experiment underlines both how useful identification is for tagging and search pipelines and how inconsistent refusals make it unreliable. Highlights - Six frontier multimodal LLMs tested on identifying public figures in images - GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4 refuse to name even Barack Obama - Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 4 Scout, Mistral Small 3.2 and Qwen 2.5-VL all identify him - On a non-notable person, all models correctly decline to hallucinate a name - Mistral's guardrail made it lie about having the ability at all - Multi-person photo: Gemini names Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg in the right order - Capability is widespread; refusal policy, not skill, is the differentiator Source Read the original story https://minimaxir.com/2025/07/llms-identify-people/ Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md · Anthropic ../entities/anthropic.md · Google ../entities/google.md · Google Gemini ../entities/gemini.md

title: A few words on DS4
text: A few words on DS4 type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high antirez anthropic deepseek agentic-systems external-evaluation ai-coding-agents compute-buildout Summary antirez reflects on DwarfStar 4's unexpected popularity: it landed at the intersection of pent-up demand for a single-model, well-integrated local AI experience, the release of a quasi-frontier open model large and fast enough to change local inference, and an extremely asymmetric 2/8-bit quantization recipe that lets 96-128GB of RAM run it. title: The AI Bubble Explained
text: The AI Bubble Explained type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Hugh Howey tackles four huge misconceptions about AI at essay length. The first - 'AI is just doing math' - he dismantles with the observation that neurons work much like logic gates with voltage differences and emergent complexity, that we don't understand consciousness or gravity well enough to be glib, and that something unprecedented is happening when ordinary life now includes dozens of daily Turing tests: math never made us ask 'is this human or synthetic?' before. On the agency question, his stance is that AI taking over our lives would be a choice, not an inevitability: you can already build a home system that frees you from your inbox, and soon it will be default - unless you don't want it. He also notes the countercurrent: people are already sick of AI everywhere, and a social platform that verifiably banned AI would draw crowds. The essay's larger aim is to replace both dismissal and panic with a clearer picture of what the 'bubble' actually contains. Highlights - Four huge AI misconceptions, argued at length - 'Just math' fails: neurons resemble logic gates, emergence is real, daily Turing tests are new - We don't understand consciousness well enough for glib dismissals - AI taking over would be a choice - inbox-free home systems already exist for those who want them - Countercurrent: AI fatigue is real; a verifiably AI-free social network would draw crowds Source Read the original story https://hughhowey.com/the-ai-bubble-explained/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: LLM Classification Is Feature Engineering
text: LLM Classification Is Feature Engineering type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-20 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai Summary This essay argues that using an LLM directly as a classifier, a prompt that returns a label, is the wrong abstraction, and that the practical fix is to treat the LLM's verdict as a feature inside an ordinary statistical model. Wrapping the LLM output in a simple logistic regression recovers the properties practitioners actually need, such as calibration to the class distribution of the population being scored, without any prompt gymnastics. Worked through on the SemEval 2018 irony-detection dataset 4,618 tweets , the one-shot LLM classifier shows decent ranking ability but a poor Brier score for lack of calibration; the logistic wrapper fixes calibration without changing the ordering. The broader point: when performance disappoints, prompt tweaking is arcane folklore, while the classic ML toolkit better features, more data, model tuning becomes available again once the LLM is demoted to feature extractor. Highlights - Core claim: an LLM's verdict should be a feature, not the classifier; wrap it in logistic regression, p y=1|x = sigma alpha + beta LLM x . - LLM classifiers lack calibration: the model cannot know whether the positive class is rare or prevalent in the tested population. - Demo dataset: SemEval 2018 Task 3, 4,618 tweets 3,834 train / 784 test labeled for irony by expert annotators. - One-shot prompting gemini-3.1-flash-lite, temperature 0, structured JSON output ranks well but calibrates poorly; random guessing scores Brier 0.25. - The logistic wrapper achieves calibration while leaving F1 unchanged, since it does not alter the ordering. - Enrichment trick: have the LLM answer auxiliary questions humor? plausibility? needs context? genuine complaint? tone mismatch and feed those as extra features. - When accuracy disappoints, prompt engineering offers folklore; the ML framing reopens feature engineering, data and model selection as levers. Source Read the original story https://minimallysufficient.com/posts/llm-classification-is-feature-extraction/ · TLDR AI issue https://tldr.tech/ai/2026-09-18 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Show HN: Mini-AGI – Dynamic continual learning model trained on 8GB VRAM
text: Show HN: Mini-AGI – Dynamic continual learning model trained on 8GB VRAM type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news anthropic Summary Mini-AGI is an experiment in continual learning: a byte-level language model that assembles its own architecture, trains from scratch on a single 8 GB VRAM GPU, and keeps learning from everything it reads. Weights are stored as ordinary files on disk and paged onto the card as needed, so the parameter count is bounded by free disk space rather than VRAM; the model grows new capacity while training when it runs short and prunes what nothing asks for. Reading and serving use exactly the same code path, so training never has to stop. The author is explicit that this is a toy-level model, not a frontier contender: the point is to show that continual learning from a single stream of data without catastrophic forgetting is possible on modest hardware, meaning almost anyone could train their own version or continue training this one. The pitch is ownership: every language model you can actually own today is a model somebody else trained and froze, fine-tunable at the edges but stopped the day it shipped. The current run is still on its first pass over the corpus; weights will be published once that pass completes, a couple of weeks away at the current rate. Highlights - Mini-AGI: byte-level continual-learning language model that assembles its own architecture. - Trains from scratch on a single 8 GB VRAM GPU; weights paged from disk, so size is bounded by disk, not VRAM. - Grows new capacity during training and prunes unused parts; reading and serving share one code path. - Author's caveat: a small toy-level model; the claim is that continual learning without catastrophic forgetting works on modest hardware. - Argument: personal models today are always someone else's frozen model with 'a thin layer of you on top'. - Weights not yet published; the run finishes its first corpus pass in a couple of weeks. - Target hardware: any PC or laptop with at least an 8 GB VRAM GPU. Source Read the original story https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/ Related pages Anthropic ../entities/anthropic.md
