title: OpenAI GPT–6 Astra breaks Enigma message that has resisted solution since 2005
text: OpenAI GPT–6 Astra breaks Enigma message that has resisted solution since 2005 type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news openai Summary Crypto Cellar Research reports the break of the German Army Enigma message MVUEH of 10 July 1941, which had resisted all attempts since 2005. Carter Leffer submitted the break on 15 September 2026 for validation, and the key and plaintext checked out immediately: the recovered key even uses a different wheel order 253 than the other known keys from that day 512 . The page's author emphasizes how the break was achieved: GPT-6 Astra did it 'entirely on its own', with Leffer only directing the model to try the unbroken Enigma messages published on the site. The 82-letter plaintext is nearly identical to that of message Nr. 173 SIPVX , broken in 2017 by Alex Shovkoplyas, differing because of an enciphering mistake Bitte became Btte and the sender's signature. The author, a self-described old cryptanalyst, says he spent weeks verifying the Bundesarchiv files the model cited and calls the result 'simply amazing'. Highlights - Enigma message MVUEH from 10 July 1941 unbroken since 2005 - Break submitted by Carter Leffer on 15 September 2026 and validated by Crypto Cellar Research - GPT-6 Astra performed the cryptanalysis 'entirely on its own', per the page - Recovered key uses wheel order 253, unlike the 512 of other keys from that day - 82-letter plaintext nearly matches message Nr. 173 SIPVX , broken in 2017 - Differences traced to an enciphering error Btte for Bitte and the sender's signature - Author says he spent weeks checking the Bundesarchiv files the model referenced Source Read the original story https://www.cryptocellar.org/bgac/the-mvueh-break.html Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md

title: What reversing, modernising old games tells us about the economic impact of AI
text: What reversing, modernising old games tells us about the economic impact of AI type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-29 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary A practitioner's meditation on what AI does to the economics of skill, told through game reverse-engineering. The author gave Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next the job of reverse-engineering and porting War of the Lance 1989 to modern browsers; it took about a week on a single-lane workstation and faithfully reproduced rendering and game rules in a new Three.js engine. He then modernized it into a Total War / Heroes of Might and Magic-style experience while keeping the original underneath - work that once meant a AAA 'total conversion' mod but is now faster to synthesize from scratch. On 3D asset creation, he finds Fable 5.1 driving Blender's headless API 'quite usable' for about 80-100 models per week of subscription, and a day later reports GPT-6 Astra clearly trained on 3D modelling, jumping from 'junior modeller' to mid-career professional. The framing observation: a doctor's 15 years of knowledge acquisition is what commands a premium - and AI compresses exactly that. Highlights - Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next reverse-engineered and ported War of the Lance 1989 to browsers in about a week - Faithful reproduction of rendering and rules in a new Three.js engine, then modernized into a Total War-style UX - Fable 5.1 + Blender headless API: ~80-100 usable 3D models per week of subscription - GPT-6 Astra is a clear step up - 'mid-career professional' 3D modelling where Fable was junior - Thesis: knowledge acquisition time is what priced skill; AI collapses that moat - Synthesizing exact features is now easier than total-conversion modding of an existing AAA game Source Read the original story https://this.os.isfine.org/blog/posts/what-reverse-engineering-and-modernising-an-old-war-game-tells-us-about-the-econ/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Evolving programming languages in the AI era
text: Evolving programming languages in the AI era type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary José Valim's ramblings on programming languages in the AI era start from a premise already true for many teams: agents write most of the code. Languages are held together by communities rallying around shared sensibilities - Python's one obvious way, Ruby's programmer happiness, Lisp's reshape-the-language ethos - and he asks what happens to that sense of belonging when humans stop writing most of the code, and whether communities should preserve it or find a new glue. On ecosystems he sees two opposing forces: agents shrink the gap between ecosystems porting implementations, translating papers and known algorithms gets cheap, so small communities catch up fast , yet the same cheapness weakens the force that creates ecosystems at all - why join a shared effort when an agent builds exactly the library you need? On syntax he is blunt: affordances like optional chaining matter far less to agents, which are unbothered by boilerplate; token efficiency is a tail-end concern as models get cheaper and contexts grow; and any new language claiming to be 'for coding agents' that focuses on syntax is building around today's limitations. From the model's perspective, he writes, it is all tokens-in, tokens-out. Highlights - Valim: agents already write most of the code for many teams - design for that reality - Language communities are glued by shared sensibilities; what replaces the glue? - Agents could shrink ecosystem gaps - porting and translating known work gets cheap - But cheap implementation also weakens the collaboration that forms ecosystems - Syntax ergonomics matter less: agents are unbothered by boilerplate - Token efficiency is a tail-end optimization as models get cheaper - Languages 'for coding agents' that focus on syntax build around today's limitations - 'From their perspective, it is all tokens-in, tokens-out' Source Read the original story https://twitter.com/josevalim/status/2103133294317445290 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

Agents connect through a CLI, MCP or typed SDKs, and background delivery lets them work without moving the user's pointer or stealing focus where the platform supports it. The headline piece is CUA-S1, a family of small 'System 1' models for fast, bounded computer-use decisions, choosing which value belongs in a field, whether to leave an element alone, rather than general planning. The first research profile targets forms, scoring decisions from structured interface elements and document values instead of generating token by token; application code orders the actions and the Cua Driver executes within explicit boundaries. Highlights - Cua: open-source desktop automation across macOS, Windows and Linux, plus cloud and local sandboxes. - Fleets at run.cua.ai provision isolated cloud desktops from a pool via the Sandbox SDK. - Background delivery lets agents operate apps without moving the pointer or taking focus platform-dependent . - CUA-S1: small 'System 1' models for fast, bounded decisions, not a replacement for a planning agent. - First profile is forms: scores decisions from structured UI elements and document values, no token-by-token generation. - MIT-licensed source; CUA-S1-FORMS weights and dataset hosted separately on Hugging Face. - Local VMs on Apple Silicon via Virtualization.Framework 'lume' installer . - Integrations for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw and others. title: The End Of Upward Mobility – AI is coming for the meritocracy
text: The End Of Upward Mobility – AI is coming for the meritocracy type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary This Noema essay reads the AI moment through James Burnham's 1941 'The Managerial Revolution', which declared capitalism finished and wrongly predicted managerial superstates, and asks what class structure AI actually threatens. Its subject is the 'homoploutic' class: households that hold both capital and high-value labor, resolving the capital-labor conflict inside the same person. The class's ideological machinery is meritocracy, per Daniel Markovits's 'The Meritocracy Trap' 2019 : an elite convinced its position is earned, even as parental investment per elite child approaches a $10 million inheritance by the end of graduate school, an M-E-M' circuit where E is the education of one's children. The double grounding in credentials and workplace performance is what gave the class political legitimacy: 'we are rich because we are useful, and you may join us if you are useful too.' AI attacks exactly that claim. The essay is honest about the unknowns, whether AI raises total output or just shifts it, whether capability progress continues given circular data-center financing and political backlash, how fast adoption lands, and locates the fork in one unresolved empirical question: whether AI will be a substitute for or a complement to high-premium cognitive labor. Two very different futures for the meritocratic class, and for everyone else, follow from the answer. Highlights - Essay in Noema: AI threatens the meritocratic 'homoploutic' class that holds both capital and elite labor. - Opens with Burnham's 1941 'Managerial Revolution' as the classic wrong prediction of capitalism's end. - Markovits's 'Meritocracy Trap': elite parental investment per child approaches a $10M inheritance by grad school. - Recasts Marx's M-C-M' as M-E-M', where E is children's education; if E becomes unreachable, mobility closes. - The class's legitimacy rests on 'we are rich because we are useful', the claim AI directly undermines. - Named unknowns: output growth vs substitution, capability progress vs circular financing, adoption speed. - The decisive question: will AI substitute for or complement high-premium cognitive labor. Source Read the original story https://www.noemamag.com/the-end-of-upward-mobility/ Related pa

title: Better Models: Worse Tools
text: Better Models: Worse Tools type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high armin-ronacher openai anthropic agentic-systems external-evaluation small-specialist-models ai-coding-agents labor-displacement Summary A strange bug in the Pi harness sent Armin Ronacher down a rabbit hole: newer Claude models - Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5, not some small variant - sometimes call the edit tool with invented extra fields in the nested edits array. The edit itself is usually correct, but the arguments do not match the schema, so Pi rejects the call and the model retries. The odd part is that this is getting worse with newer Anthropic models: older siblings do not show it, meaning the SOTA models are worse at this specific tool schema than their predecessors. The post explains how tool calling actually works under the hood: no magic, just in-band signalling where the server folds tools into the prompt with special marker tokens and the model emits something the client interprets as a call. For Anthropic models an 'ANTML' format leaks at times - not really XML, just something convenient to tokenize and train on - where string parameters appear inline but arrays of objects are JSON-serialized, a mixed convention he suspects is close to how it works. Without grammar-aware constrained decoding, the model merely follows a learned convention, and in the failing cases it invents a zoo of trailing keys: requireUnique, oldText2, newText2, type, id, kind, matchCase, forceMatchCount and more. He deliberately did not test Fable, unsure whether Anthropic's classifiers might silently downgrade him to Opus. Highlights - Newer Claude models Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5 invent extra fields in edit tool calls; older ones do not - The edit content is usually right but the schema violation makes the harness reject the call - SOTA Anthropic models are worse at this specific tool schema than their older siblings - Tool calls are crude in-band signalling: marker tokens plus learned conventions, not magic - Anthropic's 'ANTML' format leaks at times; strings inline, object arrays JSON-serialized - Without constrained decoding the model follows convention, so it hallucinates keys - Invented keys observed: requireUnique, oldText2, newText2, type, id, kind, matchCase and more - He skipped testing Fable, wary of classifiers silently downgrading him to Opus Source Read the origina

title: Write Things Down
text: Write Things Down type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high stratechery Summary Ben Thompson's 'Write Things Down' starts from David Allen's Getting Things Done and its RAM analogy: the conscious mind is a focusing tool, not a storage place, and open loops kept in short-term memory degrade it. Thompson confesses he was never conscientious enough to run the system himself, so when he hired an assistant for Stratechery, the first job was reading GTD, for Thompson's sake, not the assistant's: someone else became his inbox and task manager, keeping a perfectly organized OmniFocus he never opens. The essay then pivots to AI: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared on X that 'AGI has arrived' with GPT-6 Astra, trained on roughly 100K+ Grace Blackwell NVLink72 GPUs, his second such declaration this year. The GTD frame sets up the connection: just as Thompson outsourced remembering to a trusted person, the promise of an assistant that writes everything down and empties your RAM is what AI agents are now being sold on. Highlights - GTD's core claim: the conscious mind is for focus, not storage; open loops in 'RAM' cause distraction and worry. - Thompson was an OmniFocus beta user but 'sucked' at running the system himself. - His fix after starting Stratechery solo in 2013: hire an assistant whose first job was reading GTD for him. - Result: a perfectly organized OmniFocus he never opens; the assistant is his inbox and task manager. - Segue: Jensen Huang declared 'AGI has arrived' with GPT-6 Astra, trained on ~100K+ NVLink72 GPUs. - It is Huang's second AGI declaration this year; 400K GPUs 'coming online next', per his post. title: "As a Language Model": Chat Template Switches LLM Self-Referential Voice
text: "As a Language Model": Chat Template Switches LLM Self-Referential Voice type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-27 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary This arXiv paper shows that the chat template - the wrapper that formats prompts for instruct-tuned models - acts as a switch on how LLMs talk about themselves. With the template on, disclaimer voice 'I'm just an AI' goes up and experiential voice 'I feel' goes down; with it off, the pattern reverses. The result holds across 8 popular open-source instruct models up to 9B parameters. The authors then find a direction in the activation space of 3 models that steers this behavior: adding it increases disclaimers, removing it suppresses them, while a random direction of equal size does little. Adding the direction to a base model without a template makes it disclaim as if the template were there. Their conclusion is a methodological warning: what a model says about itself is not a fact about its weights alone - it is partly set by deployment scaffolding - so self-reports and introspection studies have a confound they need to control for, and this direction gives them a way to do it. Highlights - The chat template works like a switch on LLM self-reference: disclaimer voice up, experiential voice down - and reversed without it - Holds across 8 open-source instruct models up to 9B parameters - A steerable direction exists in activation space: add it, disclaimers rise; remove it, they fall - A random direction of the same size has little effect - the direction is specific - Base models with the direction added disclaim as if a chat template were present - Implication: model self-reports confound weights with deployment scaffolding - don't treat self-descriptions literally - The direction gives introspection and AI-safety researchers a control for the confound Source Read the original story https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25021 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: OpenAI's projected compute bill climbed to $856B
text: OpenAI's projected compute bill climbed to $856B type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high tldr-ai openai compute-buildout Summary The Financial Times reported that OpenAI expects negative free cash flow of $278 billion between 2026 and 2030, citing a July presentation prepared for a computing deal. This analysis notes the framing oddity: the same materials put revenue at $350 billion in 2030 against roughly $36 billion this year, and compute and infrastructure spending at about $856 billion across the period, up from the roughly $600 billion target given to investors publicly in February. Spending can rise while burn falls because much of the build is financed by partners rather than by OpenAI itself. The $278 billion figure is actually an improvement of about $27 billion on the roughly $305 billion negative free cash flow OpenAI projected for the same period in May, which the author argues makes the alarm framing odd: the number getting headlines is the smallest of the three, and it moved in the right direction. Samantha Oltman wrote up the figures for Bloomberg, which corrected its story shortly after publication. Highlights - FT: OpenAI projects negative free cash flow of $278B for 2026-2030, per a July presentation. - Same materials: $350B revenue in 2030 vs roughly $36B this year. - Compute and infrastructure line risen to about $856B vs the ~$600B public target from February. - Partner financing explains how spending rises while projected burn falls. - The $278B is a ~$27B improvement on May's ~$305B projection for the same period. - Bloomberg's writeup Samantha Oltman was corrected shortly after publication. - Author's point: the headline number is the smallest of the three and moved favorably. title: Show HN: Vellum, the best diagram editor you'll ever use
text: Show HN: Vellum, the best diagram editor you'll ever use type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-22 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news anthropic external-evaluation Summary In a Show HN for Vellum, a diagram editor, the author tells a debugging war story: every save of a diagram containing a new image was blocked because the app's CSP connect-src lacked the S3 origin that hosts the bytes - a third origin beyond the SPA and the API. img-src already allowed the S3 domain for displaying images, but connect-src never got the matching entry for transferring them. The bug hid behind a genuine CORS misconfiguration on the uploads bucket, because a CSP-blocked fetch fails with the same wording as a CORS-blocked one 'NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.' in Firefox, 'Failed to fetch' in Chrome - so fixing the real CORS issue did not reveal it. Highlights - Show HN: Vellum, a diagram editor, plus a CSP war story. - A missing connect-src entry for the S3 origin blocked saves with new images. - CSP- and CORS-blocked fetches fail with identical wording. - The bug hid behind a real CORS misconfiguration on the uploads bucket. - img-src had the domain; connect-src never got the match. title: NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation open-Source Geospatial AI Model
text: NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation open-Source Geospatial AI Model type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-19 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary NASA and IBM Research have released the Lunar Foundation Model, an open-source AI model pretrained from scratch on SomBench, a multimodal lunar dataset of nearly two million co-registered data bundles spanning 11 modalities and two spatial scales. It integrates imagery, topography, illumination geometry, thermophysics, mineralogy, radar and gravity data to help researchers analyze the large, diverse datasets from lunar missions, with USRA contributing planetary science expertise and evaluation. Evaluated on three downstream benchmarks, crater detection at regional and meter scales, segmentation of irregular mare patches, and regression of polar ice prospectivity, the model matched or beat ImageNet-pretrained comparisons and an identical architecture without lunar pretraining. Crater detection showed particularly strong label efficiency, and the team released the pretrained model, fine-tuning code and benchmarks openly, including a NAC crater benchmark built from more than 49,000 manually identified craters. Highlights - Pretrained from scratch on SomBench: ~2 million co-registered lunar data bundles, 11 modalities, two spatial scales. - Combines imagery, topography, illumination geometry, thermophysics, mineralogy, radar, gravity and other lunar data. - Benchmarks: crater detection regional and meter scale , irregular mare patch segmentation, polar ice prospectivity regression. - Matched or outperformed ImageNet-pretrained models and an identical architecture without lunar pretraining. - Strong label efficiency in crater detection: lunar pretraining reduces the task-specific labeled data needed. - USRA's Dr. Rachel Slank led the LROC NAC crater benchmark, manually identifying 49,000+ craters. - Pretrained model, fine-tuning code and benchmark datasets all released openly. - Announced September 18, 2026; developed under a NASA-IBM Research collaboration with USRA. Source Read the original story https://newsroom.usra.edu/usra-contributes-planetary-science-expertise-to-nasa-ibm-lunar-foundation-model/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

text: Cancer Capital: VC didn’t use to work like this type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high anil-dash google microsoft meta apple amazon gemini compute-buildout labor-displacement Summary Anil Dash illustrates how far 'Cancer Capital' - his term for the current era of venture capital - has drifted from how tech companies used to be built. title: So yeah it was written using AI
text: So yeah it was written using AI type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-26 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high bert-hubert Summary Bert Hubert pushes back on a growing habit: dismissing an article's argument outright because a detector like Pangram says the text was partly AI-authored. Hubert is no AI booster - he says he hates the origins and consequences of generative AI, wants the bubble to burst, and has publicly argued AI has gutted his own professional field. His point is narrower: choosing not to engage with AI-assisted writing is a legitimate personal choice, but declaring an article's premise wrong BECAUSE AI helped write it is a logical cop-out - and detectors can be wrong to begin with. The piece is a follow-up to an earlier essay about content served in ways readers might not like. Hubert's ask: ignore such pieces if you want, even criticize the author's ethics, but stop doing 'gotchas' that treat AI involvement as proof an argument fails. Highlights - Dismissing an argument solely because AI helped write the text is a logical cop-out, says Hubert - Pangram-style AI detectors can also simply be wrong - Refusing to engage with AI-assisted pieces is presented as a legitimate personal choice - Hubert notes his own anti-AI credentials: he rejects AI-written code contributions to his software - The post follows up an earlier piece on content served in ways readers may not like Source Read the original story https://berthub.eu/articles/posts/so-yeah-it-is-written-using-ai/ Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Big AI to humanity: drop dead
text: Big AI to humanity: drop dead type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news amazon ai-policy-regulation Summary Matthew Butterick - author, designer, programmer and lawyer - argues that the public debate about AI catastrophe is stuck in what he calls the 'Skynet fallacy': sci-fi scenarios of rogue AI that generate fear but no realistic policy paths. His own 2024 prediction was that a catastrophe from alignment failure is far more likely than one from malignant machine agency, and he sees that prediction 'ripening.' Butterick has standing beyond punditry: after learning in 2022 that his works were in generative-AI training datasets, he helped invent the first lawsuits challenging the practice and is co-counsel for plaintiffs in eight of the 142 such US cases. The essay is prompted by a run of unusual events - a US government 'statement of interest' supporting AI training as fair use in a copyright case, AI-company workers posting about human-extinction risk, and newspaper op-eds demanding that 'something' be done. Highlights - Coins the 'Skynet fallacy': media catastrophe scenarios are 'primarily a vessel for fear' and don't illuminate realistic policy change. - 142 US lawsuits now challenge the legality of training on copyrighted works; Butterick is co-counsel in eight. - The US government filed a 'statement of interest' backing AI training as fair use in a copyright case. - Butterick's 2024 view: alignment failure is a more likely catastrophe path than sci-fi malignant agency. - He declines to say whether AI companies have committed 'crimes against humanity,' keeping the essay on legal and policy ground. Source Read the original story https://matthewbutterick.com/chron/drop-dead.html Related pages Amazon ../entities/amazon.md · AI policy, regulation and litigation ../concepts/ai-policy-regulation.md

title: OpenAI reopens sign-ups for its $200/month Pro tier while halving the API credits provided per dollar to encourage pay-per-use, and removes the five-hour cap
text: OpenAI reopens sign-ups for its $200/month Pro tier while halving the API credits provided per dollar to encourage pay-per-use, and removes the five-hour cap type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-29 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high techmeme openai Summary OpenAI is reopening sign-ups for its $200/month Pro tier while halving the API credits included per dollar. Employee Thibault Sottiaux argues subscribers should still get more done than a month ago because GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna shipped this week at half their predecessors' API price. The 5-hour usage cap is gone for good, replaced by a weekly allotment subscribers can spread however they want. Strategically, the change moves OpenAI away from subsidized subscriptions toward pay-per-use: Sottiaux expects API prices to fall until there is no significant gap between subscription and API value per dollar, letting labs tie revenue to actual usage. Microsoft already does this with Copilot in places. Highlights - OpenAI reopens $200/month Pro sign-ups but halves API credits per dollar - Sottiaux: GPT-6 Sol and Luna at half price mean subscribers still get more done - The 5-hour usage cap is gone; weekly allotment can be spread freely - Signals a shift from subsidized subscriptions toward pay-per-use - Goal: API prices fall until subscription and API value per dollar converge - Microsoft already runs parts of Copilot this way Source Read the original story https://the-decoder.com/openai-reopens-its-200-pro-plan-but-cuts-api-credits-in-half-as-it-nudges-users-toward-pay-per-use/ Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md

title: I built a native Apple app for 4 platforms in one afternoon with my AI workflow
text: I built a native Apple app for 4 platforms in one afternoon with my AI workflow type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-28 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news apple Summary A developer with ADHD built ClearTime, a visual timer, as a native app across macOS, iOS, watchOS, and tvOS in about five hours from first commit to TestFlight builds, using an AI workflow. The motivation is personal: a clock tells the time but does not help him feel how much is left. The post also explains why this matters more now: at 48 he developed SVT, spent a week in the ICU with a heart rate pinned at 220 bpm, and underwent an ablation; recovery and a healthier, lower-stress life became the backdrop for building tools that reduce friction. The writeup, he jokes, took longer than the build. Highlights - Native visual timer shipped to Mac, iPhone, Apple Watch, and Apple TV in ~5 hours via an AI workflow - Built for ADHD: clocks show the time but do not convey how much is left - The author developed SVT at 48, spent a week in ICU at 220 bpm, and had an ablation - Physical visual timers inspired the idea; he wanted one that follows him across screens - TestFlight builds worked on all four platforms the same afternoon - Jokes the writeup took more time than the design and build Source Read the original story https://twitter.com/danielhayesmith/status/2103976394338271515 Related pages Apple ../entities/apple.md

title: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money
text: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-28 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols' Register column argues that the more we learn about how AI companies do business, the more unfair it looks: they must ingest everyone else's work to train their models, and they hate paying for it, obeying licenses, or sharing revenue. The fresh evidence is 404 Media's reporting on newly unsealed documents in the NYT copyright case against OpenAI and Microsoft - plaintiffs' arguments the court has not yet ruled on - in which Microsoft's own Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, is quoted calling the scraping 'an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions', possibly 'the largest theft of labor in human history.' Hecht wasn't alone: an internal Microsoft policy document, also quoted, admits generative AI could 'significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained' because 'LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.' The column's point: the industry's own scientists described the business model as theft and supply-chain destruction - while the companies kept taking the work and keeping the money. Highlights - Column: Big AI's model is 'take it now, argue about legality later' - and it's getting more blatant - Unsealed NYT-case docs via 404 Media : Microsoft scientist called the scraping 'an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions' - Also quoted: possibly 'the largest theft of labor in human history' - per the plaintiffs' brief - Internal Microsoft doc: 'LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain' - Caveat: these are plaintiffs' arguments from unsealed filings; the court has not ruled Source Read the original story https://www.theregister.com/columnists/2026/09/27/big-ais-content-problem-take-the-work-keep-the-money/5299007 Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: Show HN: Lossless-memory – a personal AI memory that never summarizes
text: Show HN: Lossless-memory – a personal AI memory that never summarizes type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high hacker-news Summary Lossless-memory is a personal AI memory system built on a refusal to summarize: most long-term memory systems either compress conversations into notes or embed and retrieve similar chunks, and both lose what actually matters to someone who talks to the same AI every day, what was actually said, and when. This project appends every conversation turn as a fixed seven-field record timestamp, actor, role, type, verbatim text, model, session to a per-day JSONL file; the raw logs are the source of truth and every index can be deleted and rebuilt from them. Time is the primary axis, not metadata: the AI can answer 'what did we decide last Tuesday night?' with the actual lines from last Tuesday night, in order. A tiny index of timestamped topic markers LLL , injected into the model's context every turn, lets a long-running assistant come back from compaction. The lineage runs from a December 2025 memory-inheritance tool through a predecessor in daily use since January 2026; this implementation has run every day since July 2026 for one user, with raw logs back to June 2026, and docs/lessons.md documents the failures. Highlights - Lossless-memory: personal AI memory that never summarizes; keeps every line with a timestamp. - Critique: summarization and embedding retrieval both lose what was actually said and when. - Seven-field record per turn: ts, actor, role, type, verbatim text, model, session; per-day JSONL files. - Raw logs are the source of truth; all indexes are rebuildable and disposable. - Time as primary axis: answer 'what did we decide last Tuesday night?' with the actual lines. - LLL: tiny timestamped topic-marker index injected into context every turn to survive compaction. - In daily use since July 2026 for one user; lineage back to December 2025; failures documented in docs/lessons.md. Source Read the original story https://github.com/aru-labs/lossless-memory Related pages No related entity or concept page yet.

title: OpenAI: 'fully autonomous RSI is not happening today'
text: OpenAI: 'fully autonomous RSI is not happening today' type: news-summary · created: 2026-09-21 · updated: 2026-09-30 · confidence: high techmeme openai ai-policy-regulation Summary OpenAI lays out its position on the next phase of AI development: as automated AI research takes over more of the work of building successive model generations, recursive self-improvement RSI could accelerate progress rapidly even while people remain involved. The company frames its mission around three goals - building an automated AI researcher while iterating on the alignment problem, delivering the economic benefits of very intelligent machines, and empowering individuals with a personal AGI - and argues alignment research must keep pace with capabilities. The post stresses that capable, aligned AI is itself part of the safety answer, strengthening defenses and advancing alignment research, and calls for shared standards to guide development across labs and countries. Notably, OpenAI states that fully autonomous RSI is 'not happening today', positioning gradual, supervised automation of research as the manageable path rather than an abrupt intelligence explosion. Highlights - OpenAI: fully autonomous recursive self-improvement RSI 'is not happening today' - Three stated goals: build an automated AI researcher and iterate on alignment; deliver scientific and economic benefits; empower everyone with a personal AGI - Warns that as AI drives more of its own R&D, the pace of progress could accelerate rapidly even with humans in the loop - Argues alignment research must keep pace with capabilities as systems grow more autonomous - Calls for shared standards to guide development across labs and countries - Frames capable, aligned AI as part of the defense against the risks of the transition itself Source Read the original story https://openai.com/index/building-standards-next-phase-ai/ Related pages OpenAI ../entities/openai.md · AI policy, regulation and litigation ../concepts/ai-policy-regulation.md
